goals.name: Usability & Efficiency
goals.description: How well a system helps users achieve goals quickly, clearly, and without mistakes. In gamification, efficiency ensures that playful features (points, badges, challenges) add value rather than confusion. Recommended instruments: AttrakDiff, UEQ, meCUE.

goals.name: Guidance & Feedback
goals.description: The quality of information the system provides to help users understand what is happening and how well they are performing. In gamification, feedback mechanics such as progress bars and scores are central — timely, specific, and meaningful feedback drives learning. Recommended instruments: SUS, UMUX, meCUE.

goals.name: Novelty / Curiosity
goals.description: How exciting, curious, and engaging a product feels. Varied challenges, surprise rewards, and evolving mechanics prevent habituation and sustain long-term engagement. Recommended instruments: AttrakDiff, UEQ, GEQ.

goals.name: Aesthetic & Attractiveness
goals.description: The visual and sensory appeal of a product. A visually polished system signals craftsmanship and care, increasing user confidence and enjoyment of the experience. Recommended instruments: AttrakDiff, VisAWI, UEQ.

goals.name: Affective Experience
goals.description: The emotional states arising during interaction: joy, excitement, and pride on the positive side; frustration, anxiety, and boredom on the negative. Reward systems and feedback loops should be calibrated to optimize the emotional balance. Recommended instruments: SAM, PANAS, GEQ.

goals.name: Tension / Pressure
goals.description: The psychological stress or urgency users feel. Moderate tension increases excitement and engagement, but excessive pressure leads to disengagement. Challenge mechanics and time limits must be carefully calibrated. Recommended instruments: GEQ, NASA-TLX, SAM.

goals.name: Competence / Mastery
goals.description: The feeling of being effective and skilled. Progressive difficulty, skill-based challenges, and clear performance feedback support competence. Badges, levels, and leaderboards reinforce mastery when designed thoughtfully. Recommended instruments: PENS, IMI, BNS.

goals.name: Autonomy / Perceived Choice
goals.description: The sense of control and self-direction. Providing real choices — branching paths, customizable goals, flexible progressions — deepens personal investment and avoids the feeling of being coerced. Recommended instruments: PENS, IMI, BNS.

goals.name: Social Connection / Relatedness
goals.description: The sense of belonging and community. Social mechanics like guilds, leaderboards, collaborative challenges, and social sharing amplify motivation and long-term engagement. Designing for positive social dynamics while avoiding toxic competition is key. Recommended instruments: PENS, Social Presence Scale, GEQ.

goals.name: Motivation Spectrum
goals.description: Ranges from purely external motivation (earning points for rewards) to fully internal motivation (playing because it is genuinely enjoyable and meaningful). Gameful design aims to move users toward more autonomous forms. Over-reliance on extrinsic rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation — known as the overjustification effect. Recommended instruments: IMI, SMS, BREQ.

goals.name: Behavioral Impact
goals.description: Measures how gamification affects actual user actions and habits over time. Behavioral metrics capture whether the system genuinely changes behavior — completion rates, return visits, goal achievement — beyond self-reported attitudes. Recommended instruments: BREQ, IMI, Goal Attainment Scale.

goals.name: Progress / Accomplishment
goals.description: The sense of advancement as users move through a system. XP bars, levels, streaks, and achievement unlocks are among the most effective drivers of continued engagement — provided the progress feels earned and meaningful, not arbitrary. Recommended instruments: FSS-2, GEQ, EGameFlow.

goals.name: Engagement
goals.description: The depth and quality of involvement — going beyond mere usage to genuine absorption, interest, and investment. Multi-layered challenges, meaningful choices, and social dynamics combine to create systems that hold attention and build lasting habits. Recommended instruments: UES, GEQ, O'Brien & Toms Scale.

goals.name: Immersion / Flow / Focused Attention
goals.description: Flow is a state of optimal experience in which a person is fully immersed, losing track of time and self-consciousness. It requires balance between challenge and skill. Adaptive difficulty, clear goals, and immediate feedback all contribute to flow-inducing experiences. Recommended instruments: FSS-2, EGameFlow, GEQ.

goals.name: Personal Meaning & Relevance
goals.description: How well an experience aligns with users' personal goals and values. When users see an activity as meaningful, they are far more likely to sustain engagement over time. Recommended instruments: miniPXI, MEEGA+, IMI.

goals.name: Purpose & Values Alignment
goals.description: The degree to which an experience supports users' broader life goals. When a gamified system aligns with what users care about — self-improvement, learning, helping others — it transitions from entertainment to genuine enrichment. Recommended instruments: miniPXI, SDT Scale, GEQ.

goals.name: Self-Transcendence
goals.description: Experiences that extend beyond personal gain — contributing to something larger, connecting with others, or achieving a sense of legacy. Cooperative challenges and prosocial mechanics can trigger these transcendent experiences. Recommended instruments: PERMA Scale, miniPXI, Character Strengths Survey.

stages.name: Concept / idea
stages.description: Early exploration phase. Expert reviews, personas, and interviews are ideal for validating assumptions before any resource is committed to building.

stages.name: Low-fidelity prototype
stages.description: Paper sketches or simple wireframes. Think-aloud sessions and focus groups can surface usability issues at very low cost.

stages.name: High-fidelity prototype
stages.description: Interactive, near-final interfaces. Structured usability tests and validated questionnaires become applicable for the first time.

stages.name: Deployed system
stages.description: Live product with real users. Longitudinal methods like diary studies, surveys, and behavioral analytics capture actual usage patterns and satisfaction over time.

methods.name: Think-aloud testing
methods.description: Users verbalize thoughts while interacting with the system to surface usability issues in real time.

methods.name: Surveys & Questionnaires
methods.description: Collect structured user feedback through standardized questionnaires measuring attitudes, satisfaction, and engagement.

methods.name: Heuristic evaluation
methods.description: Experts inspect the interface against established usability principles to identify design problems.

methods.name: Expert review
methods.description: A focused expert inspection of the proposed experience and interaction flow at concept level.

methods.name: Interview
methods.description: A structured or semi-structured conversation with users to explore their experiences, emotions, and opinions in depth.

methods.name: Observation
methods.description: Watching users interact with the system in their natural context, without intervention, to capture authentic behaviors.

methods.name: Focus Group
methods.description: A moderated group discussion (typically 6–10 users) to explore shared perceptions, social dynamics, and community experiences.

methods.name: Diary Study
methods.description: Participants self-report their experiences, behaviors, and motivations over an extended period to capture longitudinal patterns.

methods.name: Experience Report
methods.description: Accounts written or recorded by users after interacting with the system, reflecting on their overall experience.

instruments.name: Task based protocol
instruments.description: Guide user through specific tasks to identify usability issues in a structured way.
attributes: Recommended for quick, focused usability evaluations

instruments.name: Think-Aloud script
instruments.description: Facilitator script instructing users to think aloud and guiding session flow.

instruments.name: Observation Grid
instruments.description: Structured note-taking sheet for recording observed usability issues and user behaviours.

instruments.name: Heuristic Checklist
instruments.description: A checklist derived from recognised usability and game UX heuristics for systematic expert inspection.

instruments.name: UMUX-Lite
instruments.description: Measure perceived usability with 2 items — fast and validated for any context.
attributes: Suited for time-constrained or small-sample evaluations

instruments.name: SUS
instruments.description: 10-item System Usability Scale — the most widely used standardised usability questionnaire.
attributes: Better suited for comprehensive evaluations with normative benchmarking

instruments.name: AttrakDiff
instruments.description: Semantic differential scale measuring pragmatic qualities, hedonic qualities, and overall attractiveness.
attributes: Covers both usability and aesthetic dimensions

instruments.name: UEQ
instruments.description: User Experience Questionnaire — measures attractiveness, perspicuity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation, and novelty.

instruments.name: meCUE
instruments.description: Modular Evaluation of Key Components of User Experience — covers usefulness, usability, visual aesthetics, and emotions.
attributes: Modular design — use only relevant subscales
Covers both instrumental and non-instrumental qualities

instruments.name: GEQ
instruments.description: Game Experience Questionnaire — measures immersion, flow, competence, tension, challenge, and positive/negative affect.
attributes: Purpose-built for game and gamification contexts

instruments.name: SAM
instruments.description: Self-Assessment Manikin — a non-verbal pictorial scale measuring valence, arousal, and dominance.

instruments.name: PANAS
instruments.description: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule — measures the intensity of positive and negative emotional states.
attributes: Sensitive to both pre/post interaction changes

instruments.name: NASA-TLX
instruments.description: NASA Task Load Index — multidimensional workload scale measuring mental demand, physical demand, and frustration.

instruments.name: PENS
instruments.description: Player Experience of Need Satisfaction — measures competence, autonomy, and relatedness satisfaction in play contexts.

instruments.name: IMI
instruments.description: Intrinsic Motivation Inventory — measures interest/enjoyment, perceived competence, autonomy, relatedness, and effort.
attributes: Covers the full intrinsic-extrinsic motivation spectrum

instruments.name: BNS
instruments.description: Basic Need Satisfaction Scale — measures the degree to which autonomy, competence, and relatedness needs are met.

instruments.name: FSS-2
instruments.description: Flow State Scale — measures the nine dimensions of flow as described by Csikszentmihalyi.

instruments.name: EGameFlow
instruments.description: E-Learning Game Flow Scale — measures flow in educational game contexts across concentration, goal clarity, and feedback.
attributes: Includes goal clarity and challenge-skill balance subscales

instruments.name: UES
instruments.description: User Engagement Scale — measures focused attention, felt involvement, aesthetic appeal, and reward dimensions of engagement.

instruments.name: miniPXI
instruments.description: Mini Player Experience Inventory — a brief scale measuring meaning, purpose, and transcendence in game experiences.
attributes: Covers eudaimonic dimensions rarely addressed by other scales

instruments.name: MEEGA+
instruments.description: Model for Evaluation of Educational Games — measures usability, fun, and learning experience in educational game contexts.
attributes: Covers both UX quality and learning outcomes
